text.p: The following are some of the leading stories in Finnish papers this morning.
- 1997 will be a decisive year in lowering unemployment, President Martti Ahtisaari said in his New Year's speech.
- Finns are more hopeful than most other Europeans, with 39 percent in a Suomen Gallup poll expecting a better new year against 11 percent expecting a worse year.
- Uudenmaankatu in central Helsinki has become an international catwalk for trendy youth.
- New cars must from the turn of the year have a device keeping engine from working unless they are started with a proper ignition key.
- Domestic bus and train travel costs more this year: train fares up 1.8 percent and bus tickets up 4.5 percent on average.

- Finnish Forest Research Institute Metla has made a detailed map over Finland's forests combining techniques of land and satellite measurement. The map has the world's closest detail of 25 metres by 25 metres.
- Finnish monetary policy is too tight and there is a real risk of deflation, says Pertti Parmanne, chief economist at the Central Union of Finnish Trade Unions (SAK).
- President Martti Ahtisaari said in his New Year's speech that joblessness means Finland is threatened by division into three classes -- winners, those in uncertainty and losers.

- 'Komet Bomb 3' fireworks injured over 30 in New Year festivities, blowing up in users' faces, causing some severe eye injury. Product labelled "for professional use only" was sold in normal retail outlets.

- Leftists and Social Democrats should recover from mood of defeat after losses in autumn European and local elections, so government can step up pace of its work, says Eva Biaudet, chairman of the Swedish Peoples' Party's parliamentary group.
- President Martti Ahtisaari in his New Year's speech warned of social displacement which could lead to extreme anti-social phenomena.

- Prospect of ending duty-free sales on passenger ferries between Finland and Sweden puts countries' shipping industries in jeopardy. Lower passenger volumes could mean higher ticket prices and cargo fees, even reduce profitability of foreign trade.
